questions.stem: A **property** of a material tells us…
questions.explanation: A property describes what a material is like, for example hard, shiny or waterproof. Every material has its own properties.

questions.stem: Match each property word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: These property words help us describe materials. A towel is absorbent, a raincoat is waterproof and a window is transparent.

questions.stem: Opposite words: shiny and ___; flexible and ___.
questions.explanation: A shiny material reflects light, so its opposite is dull. A flexible material bends easily, so its opposite is stiff.

questions.stem: All metals are attracted by a magnet.
questions.explanation: A magnet attracts iron and steel (and a few others such as nickel). Aluminium, copper, gold and silver are metals that a magnet does not attract.

questions.stem: Sort these materials into hard and soft.
questions.explanation: Hard materials do not dent when you press them. Soft materials squash easily.

questions.stem: A magnet attracts things made of ___ and steel.
questions.explanation: Magnetic materials are iron and steel. Wood, plastic and copper are not magnetic.

questions.stem: A magnet is held near each object. Which objects will it pull? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Iron and steel are magnetic, so the nail, the paper clip and the pin are pulled. Aluminium and plastic are not magnetic.

questions.stem: Glass is used for windows because it is…
questions.explanation: Glass is transparent, so light comes in and we can see out. Wood is opaque, so it would block the light.

questions.stem: A paper umbrella would be a good idea for the monsoon.
questions.explanation: Paper is absorbent and weak. It would get soggy and tear in the rain. An umbrella needs a waterproof material.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a fair test in order to find which material soaks up the most water.
sequence: Cut a square of the same size from each material.
Pour the same amount of water into each dish.
Put one square into each dish for one minute.
Lift the squares out and measure the water left in each dish.
Work out how much water each material soaked up.
questions.explanation: A fair test keeps everything the same (size, water, time) except the material. The water left tells you how much was soaked up.

questions.stem: Why is a window made of glass and not wood?
questions.model_answer: Glass is transparent, so light comes in and we can see through it. Wood is opaque and blocks the light.
questions.explanation: Windows must let light in, so they need a transparent material. Wood is opaque: you cannot see through it.

questions.stem: Jute is used to make sacks and rope because the fibres are…
questions.explanation: Jute fibres are strong and flexible, so they can be twisted into rope and woven into sacks and bags.

questions.stem: A material that soaks up water is ___. A material that keeps water out is ___.
questions.explanation: A towel is absorbent, so it soaks up water. A plastic raincoat is waterproof, so water stays outside.

questions.stem: Which picture shows something **transparent**?
questions.explanation: You can see through the glass in a window, so it is transparent. A door, a brick and a log are opaque: you cannot see through them.

questions.stem: A magnet is held over these pictures. Which one will it pick up?
questions.explanation: A paper clip is made of steel, and steel is magnetic. Feathers, plastic and wood are not magnetic.

questions.stem: Match each picture to the material it is mostly made of.
questions.explanation: Everyday objects are made from materials such as clay, glass, paper, cloth and metal.

questions.stem: Sort these things into magnetic and not magnetic.
questions.explanation: Paper clips, safety pins and sewing needles are made of steel, so a magnet attracts them. Plastic, feathers, wood and glass are not magnetic.

questions.stem: Which picture shows something that is both **hard** and **opaque**?
questions.explanation: A brick is hard and you cannot see through it. A sponge and yarn are soft, and a window is hard but transparent.

questions.stem: Mina is going to the bazar. She wants a strong bag that rots away safely when it is thrown out. Which bag should she take?
options: a bag made of cotton wool
questions.explanation: Jute is strong and rots away in the soil. A thin plastic bag stays for hundreds of years and can block drains.

questions.stem: It is the monsoon. Anika needs a coat for the walk to school. Which material is best for the outside of the coat?
questions.explanation: A raincoat must keep water out, so its outer layer must be waterproof. Wool, paper and towel cloth soak up water.

questions.stem: Imran drops a steel needle into a pile of sand. What is the quickest way to find it?
options: Move a magnet over the sand.
Wave a plastic ruler over the sand.
Shine a torch on the sand.
questions.explanation: Steel is magnetic, so the needle jumps to the magnet. Sand is not magnetic and stays behind.

questions.stem: A pot for cooking rice on a stove needs the right material. Which properties does the material need? Choose all that are right.
options: does not melt on a stove
questions.explanation: A cooking pot must be strong and must not melt on the stove. An absorbent or easily broken pot would be no use.

questions.stem: Farmers in Bangladesh store rice in jute sacks. Jute is a good material for sacks because the fibres are strong.
questions.explanation: Strong fibres do not tear easily, so jute sacks can hold heavy rice and be used again and again.

questions.stem: Class 3A put a 10 cm square of each material into 50 ml of water for one minute. Water left in the dish: cotton towel 20 ml, paper towel 30 ml, newspaper 40 ml, plastic 50 ml. Which statement is correct?
options: The plastic soaked up the most: 50 ml.
The paper towel soaked up more than the cotton towel.
The cotton towel soaked up the most: 30 ml.
questions.explanation: Water soaked up = 50 ml minus water left. Cotton towel 30 ml, paper towel 20 ml, newspaper 10 ml, plastic 0 ml. The plastic left all 50 ml behind, so it soaked up nothing.

questions.stem: Lina tests which cloth soaks up the most water. She puts a 10 cm square of cotton in 50 ml of water and a 20 cm square of wool in 100 ml of water. Why is this not a fair test?
options: She should have used only one cloth in the whole test.
She changed the size of the cloth and the amount of water, not only the material.
She used cloth instead of paper in the test.
She should have used no water in the test.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing changes (here the material). Size, amount of water and time must stay the same.

questions.stem: Aisha says: "A coin is made of metal, so a magnet will always pick it up." Aisha is right.
questions.explanation: Some coins contain steel and stick to a magnet, but others are made of metals that are not magnetic. You must test each one.

questions.stem: A builder needs a material for a footbridge over a canal. Which properties must it have? Give two.
questions.model_answer: It must be strong and stiff, and waterproof or not rot or rust in water.
questions.explanation: A bridge carries heavy loads, so it must be strong and stiff. It also stays outdoors in rain, so it must not rot or rust easily.

questions.stem: Four things are tested with a magnet. Which one is the odd one out?
questions.explanation: The nail, the pin and the paper clip are made of iron or steel, so a magnet attracts them. Aluminium is not magnetic.
